Dear Customer Services,



I am writing to raise a formal complaint regarding the advertising agreement I entered into with Yell in November, at a cost of £298.80 per month.



From the outset, the service has failed to deliver what was represented during the sales process. Since the agreement began, I have received no business leads whatsoever that can be attributed to Yell, which represents a complete lack of return on what is a significant monthly cost to my business.



Furthermore, at the beginning of the agreement I was promised an induction call/meeting in which I would be guided through the service and advised on how best to optimise the advertising and maximise enquiries. This induction never took place, meaning I was never given any professional guidance regarding the setup, content, or input required from my side in order for the advertising to perform effectively.



This failure at the very start of the agreement raises serious concerns about whether the service has ever been properly implemented.



My experience with customer support has also been extremely disappointing. During a phone call today with a member of your team, Rash, I explained that I wished to terminate the agreement due to the total absence of results. Rather than attempting to address the issue or escalate the complaint, I was simply told that the contract was for one year and could not be cancelled, after which the call was abruptly ended.



This level of service and handling of a customer complaint is not acceptable.



In addition, I must highlight that the service being delivered appears materially different from the service that was represented to me during the sales process. The agreement was entered into on the understanding that Yell’s advertising platform would actively generate customer enquiries for my business and that I would receive onboarding support to help optimise the listing. Given that no leads have been generated and the promised induction support was never provided, I am concerned that there has been a significant failure between the sales representation and the service actually delivered. I therefore request that this be reviewed as part of your formal complaints and compliance process.



Given:



The complete absence of leads or measurable return,
The failure to deliver the promised induction and onboarding support, and
The unsatisfactory response from your team when raising these issues,




I am formally requesting that this agreement be terminated without further financial obligation.



I must also state that, based on the difference between what was represented during the sales process and what has actually been delivered, I am concerned that the agreement may have been mis-sold. I would therefore ask that this matter be reviewed by your compliance or senior complaints team as part of this formal complaint.



If this matter cannot be resolved promptly, I will consider escalating the issue further, including submitting a complaint to the Advertising Standards Authority regarding the representations made during the sales process, and raising the matter with Trading Standards in relation to the service that has been delivered.



Please treat this message as a formal complaint and request for contract review. I would appreciate a written response within 7 days from a senior member of your customer services or account management team confirming how this matter will be resolved.



If I do not receive a satisfactory response within this timeframe, I will have little option but to review and formally dispute any further payments associated with this agreement while the complaint is under investigation.



Regards

Lee Davies

Countrywide Shutters

I rarely leave negative reviews, but Bark’s customer service genuinely shocked me.

I spent over £100 on credits and didn’t get a single job from them. They refunded the credits back to my Bark account, which is apparently their policy, but completely refused to refund the money back to my original payment method.

Normally I’d accept that, but I explained my circumstances. I’d recently lost my job, was going through a formal grievance, and was facing serious financial hardship. I wasn’t asking for anything unreasonable - I simply asked them to make an exception so I could access money I’d already paid while I got back on my feet. I even told them I fully intended to come back and use Bark again once my situation had improved.

Instead, I got the same copy-and-paste policy response over and over again. No empathy. No understanding. No willingness to exercise any discretion whatsoever.

Policies exist for a reason, but good customer service is about recognising when exceptional circumstances deserve an exceptional response. Bark had every opportunity to show a bit of humanity and chose not to.

If you’re happy dealing with a company that sticks rigidly to policy regardless of the situation their customers are in, then Bark may be fine for you. Personally, I’ll remember how I was treated when I needed understanding the most.

I rarely leave negative reviews, but my experience with Yell has been extremely disappointing and ongoing.

I paid for their website design service at the beginning of December last year. Since then, the website has never been properly completed, never fully went live, and was never even transferred over to my correct domain name.

In the months that followed, the only contact I received was from third-party businesses attempting to sell me additional products and services — not meaningful updates or support regarding my own website.

IN NEARLY 6 MONTHS I HAVEN'T HAD ***ONE**** LEAD

To put this into perspective, my own self-built Wix website continues to generate significantly more daily traffic than anything Yell has produced, despite this being a service costing thousands per year.

More recently, I have spent the past three weeks trying to get basic amendments made so that my studio’s website can finally function as intended. Nothing has been actioned. Responses take over a week, when they come at all, and the delays now feel excessive and unjustified.

I raised a formal complaint via email last week using the address provided and, to date, I have received no response whatsoever.

This is not an isolated issue either — my husband experienced similar problems with his own website through Yell.

At this stage, I am exploring options to recover my money through Trading Standards and other routes, as I do not feel the service delivered reflects what was promised or paid for.

I would strongly advise others to proceed with caution before committing to Yell’s website services.

My experience with Yell has been financially damaging, emotionally draining, and riddled with systemic failures across almost every department I dealt with.

Apologies to Conor the account manager for having to write this.  He was a very nice and helpful guy.  The failings are systematic and nothing to do with him. 

I signed up for what was sold to me as a performance-based acquisition system designed to bring in paying customers. That was repeated across multiple calls and never corrected. In reality, what I received was a stream of low-quality, irrelevant enquiries that did not match the service I provide. This was completely different from the product that was advertised and sold to me.

Over six months, I paid approximately £6,000 for a service that failed on every level:

▪ Zero proactive campaign management

Ads were left switched off for long periods without anyone noticing.
When I asked why basic marketing fundamentals were missing (retargeting, exclusions, lookalikes, job-title targeting), I was told ads are “not proactively managed unless clients complain.” That alone speaks volumes.

▪ Wrong targeting and wrong messaging

Despite providing detailed instructions again and again, Yell repeatedly advertised the wrong message, the wrong offer, and targeted the wrong regions and demographics.

▪ Severe billing issues

Yell took duplicate payments, charged more months than agreed, and then told me to sort it out through my bank - something no reputable company should ever tell a customer. Months later, key refunds still were not resolved.

▪ Complete breakdown in communication

I raised multiple formal complaints.
Not one was acknowledged or responded to within the timeframes they themselves set.
Even now, they have not provided the required resolutions.

▪ Massive impact on my business

Before using Yell, my coaching business was stable with strong client numbers.
After months of failed delivery, wasted ad spend, mismanagement, and time spent correcting their errors, my business fell into serious financial distress.

I was forced to run my own ads at £5/day just to stay visible, because I had no budget left - all my capital was tied up in a system that did not function.

▪ Hours of my own time wasted

I spent countless hours writing emails, rewriting ad copy, guiding their staff, reviewing errors, submitting complaints, and trying to help them deliver the product I had already paid for. None of this work should ever fall on the client.

The only positive

Conor, the account manager, was polite and made genuine efforts - but even he was blocked by Yell’s broken internal systems. The problem is not staff like him. The problem is the structure, the lack of capability, and the systemic failures in the organisation.

Bottom line:

Yell sold me one thing, delivered something completely different, mishandled my payments, ignored my complaints, damaged my business, and wasted months of my time.

I cannot recommend strongly enough that businesses avoid Yell.

There are far better marketing services out there, and many far cheaper ones that will still outperform what I received.

As Yell have not responded or acknowledged my official complaint emails I have had to raise with the ASA, Trading Standards, ICO, CMA and prepare for small claims court.  I appreciate the polite response Penny however I’ve tried to settle this amicably for months now.

The problem is, you’re not guaranteed to get any leads that result in actual work. I really don’t like it because it feels like every time you spend money to get credits, you’re just rolling the dice, hoping that someone bites.

It gets worse though, because if someone actually contacts you and requests a quote, you STILL have to pay to be able to communicate with them, and even then, you’re not guaranteed to get the job. 

It’s a gamble every time you buy credits, and I really don’t like throwing money at something that isn’t guaranteed to work. If I wanted to do that, I would just risk my hard-earned money by betting on horses.

In conclusion, I don’t recommend this platform. You’re better off doing jobs for family and friends to begin with and build a foundation, then let word of mouth do the rest.

Not for small growing businesses. This will be an in-depth explanation of what I learned from one year with Yell and how yell will keep you trapped at a high price for their services,  leading to small business growth stunting.

TLDR- You won't own your website. The SEO is not good. Barely any leads from yell. Gaslighting and misleading sales pitches. A phone number extension that makes your backlinks unless once you leave yell.

I have a basic background in website design and SEO but went back to a service business. On the first phone call my website was ripped apart and told no one would find it then I was shown a graph of how many more people visit yell that other lead providers so that's how I would get leads (only later when in the contract they tell you they can't guarantee leads). I needed leads and it was made out that my website would be better. 
Down the line I had to redesign my website and fix SEO as it didn't hit any of the services I specifically asked to focus on. I've had to do extra work to fix the SEO so I can get viewed when people search for the terms my business relates to. 
-I called to complain several times about the lack of leads through yell. Yell have an extra "£300p/m" worth of marketing added to attempt to fix this. Nothing changed. I have watched closely the leads that come through yell and those other lead providers that I was shown on the graph initially. Even though I was top in many areas and on several services during my time with the extra marketing with yell I was having barely any leads while I watched many regularly come through other lead providers. This would indicate a misleading pitch by yell that did not apply to me and my area of services. 
-Because of the high cost (to a small business) of this service by yell and lack of leads, it forced me to have to market in other ways to make up the money I needed to pay to yell. I worked out in total that I didn't even make back 1/3rd of the total cost I paid to yell over a year, meaning a loss of 2/3rds the total cost. This was the only marketing I had a loss on over the year and I could have been much more ahead if I had used other marketing options rather than yell. Keep in mind I have several services I can market for, others may struggle more if they rely on 1 service.
-On cancelling the contract your website will get cut off, yell doesn't build you a website like other companies, they rent it to you meaning you have to stay with them at a high cost to keep the website. 
-On one phone call it was attempted gaslighting to say that my chosen marketing wouldn't work yet I was receiving regular jobs from that marketing and barely any from yell. 
-They will add a phone number extension for tracking calls. This was later used to again gaslight me to say how many leads yell was getting me, it was actually coming from the work I had previously put into my google, socials and advertising that had nothing to do with yell. I regularly checked where people found me and rarely did anyone answer yell. The extension number also had bad connection making it difficult to converse with customers, also looking highly unprofessional. My mobile number, which I used in other places to track the difference in lead numbers, never had a delay or connection issue. This extension number is what they will list on all the backlinks to the website meaning the backlinks are only useful while you are with yell. As soon as you cancel all that money you spent with them goes down the drain.

My recommendation- Get a website built by a company who specialise in building and doing SEO but ultimately you own the website and pay for ongoing hosting costs and domain name only. Don't allow anyone to add an extension number that you don't personally own so that your site cant be held hostage by a company. Look up professional reviews of yell to see how they operate.

I had been a customer of for around 18 months and always paid on time. I then entered into a new agreement for the Accelerate Tier 5 package with SEO bolt-on at a cost of approximately £2,549 per month plus VAT.

The package was sold heavily around Yell’s “Guaranteed Leads” proposition, which is advertised prominently across their website and sales material as “The UK’s only digital marketing agency that guarantees leads” The package breakdown presented to me was approximately:
• £1,600 Google Ads
• £800 Sponsored Listings
• £450 SEO

Based on those representations, my understanding was that the Google Ads(later discovered via GOTU, white label marketing- not proper Google campaign management as sold) allocation represented substantial actual advertising spend into Google campaigns, while the Sponsored Listings element related to advertising on Yell’s own platform.

However, over time I became increasingly concerned about the transparency of the package, the operation of the Lead Guarantee, and the actual allocation of advertising spend.

The biggest issue for me is that the reality of how the package appears to operate is very different from the impression created during the sales process and marketing. The Yell Web site has it big and bold "The UK’s only digital marketing agency that guarantees leads" Then the live chat pops up and big and bold "Guaranteed Leads, Exclusive to Yell"

For example:
• I later discovered that “margin fees” were embedded within the Google Ads allocation itself
• These management/margin fees were never separately itemised or visibly disclosed to me during the sales process
• The actual media spend versus retained management fees was never transparently reported but is understood to be around 50%. So £1600 Google Ad spend is actually £800 Google Ad spend and £800 for Yell Google Ad management.(This fee is important when we get to the performance)
• The Lead Guarantee itself appears subject to extensive conditions and internal reporting controls that are not obvious from the headline marketing claims.
In simple terms, the “Lead Guarantee” appears to mean:
Yell decide how leads are counted
Yell control the reporting
You still have to pay even if the guarantee is missed
Any credit is usually applied later, not automatically refunded
The guarantee is based on their calculations and definitions, not necessarily what a customer would view as a genuine lead
So while it is technically a “guarantee,” it operates more like:
a conditional account credit system controlled by Yell’s own terms and reporting.

I also formally raised concerns during the live agreement regarding lead delivery, reporting discrepancies, and lead quality. Despite this, no credit was ever disclosed or applied to my account at the time. It was only much later, during collections activity, (5 months later) that Yell alleged a credit had internally been calculated.

Another major concern was campaign performance itself. Yell’s own figures later disclosed over 22,000 clicks resulting in only 8 conversions (click to call, click to email or a form fill), with conversion costs exceeding £1,500 each over a 4 month reporting period. By comparison, my independently managed campaigns are currently achieving significantly stronger results at a fraction of the cost at 26 conversions at £48 per conversion during a 1 month reporting period. (These 26 conversions cost less than one conversion from Yell) The same 26 conversions would cost me £39,000 with Yell where as it costs £1248 with my new managed campaign. This leads to the 50% Google Ad management fee of £800. Are Yell qualified? Results would suggest, "Unlikely"

There were also periods at the start of the agreement where parts of the advertising setup reportedly could not connect properly to Facebook/social campaigns, yet full billing continued and no reconciliation or adjustment of advertising allocation was ever provided.

My concern is that the practical operation of this package, the Lead Guarantee, and the transparency around spend allocation were materially different from the impression created by the sales process and marketing.

Consider the following actions:
• Get a a full written breakdown of actual media spend versus management fees
• Ask exactly how leads are classified and counted (missed calls, supplier calls, same number calling you)
• Ask what happens operationally if the Lead Guarantee is missed. Ask for written clarification on the process via email.
• Request direct platform reporting from Google Ads itself to see your spend v margin/management fees
• Read the full terms and conditions very carefully before signing

This package is far more complex and conditional than the headline “Guaranteed Leads” marketing suggests

When I joined Checkatrade over 10 years ago, I couldn’t rate it highly enough. Now it is no longer for the tradesperson. It costs 3 times as much and airs more on the side of the homeowner! Customer service is poor as well!

I chose a decorator exclusively because of their Checkatrade profile. The business had around 50 overwhelmingly positive reviews, almost all 10/10, which gave me the confidence to hand over the keys to my newly purchased home.

The workmanship I received was completely inconsistent with that reputation. I was left with defective decorating work, damage to my property and significant costs to have everything put right.

What has disappointed me even more is Checkatrade's handling of the complaint. Although they confirmed they would investigate the workmanship and the trader's conduct, they repeatedly focused on whether I had proof of payment. In my case, no payment was made because, after I challenged the quality of the work, the trader refused payment himself and said he would leave the work "as a gift."

Despite this unusual situation, I have still suffered financial loss and have been left with the cost of rectifying the damage. I also raised concerns about the significant discrepancy between the trader I encountered and the reputation presented on the Checkatrade profile, but I have received very little information about the investigation or what steps are being taken to protect other customers.

The value of a platform like Checkatrade is trust. Customers rely on the reviews, the vetting process and the reassurance that concerns will be investigated thoroughly when things go wrong. Unfortunately, my experience has left me questioning how much protection customers actually receive when a trader's work falls so far below the standard represented on the platform.

Update: After receiving a response from Bark here asking me to contact them directly so they could review my account, I did exactly that.

I first received a generic template response. I replied, reminding them that they had specifically offered to review my account. I then received another generic response explaining how their credit refund system works.

I’ve used Bark for around two years. I’m fully aware of how the credit refund process works, and in my experience refund requests are almost never approved—which is one of the reasons I wrote this review in the first place.

Unfortunately, this leaves me feeling that the public response here was simply for show, rather than a genuine attempt to investigate my concerns, so I can’t change my review.

To clarify, my main concern is that Bark now states they have confirmed with the customer that they still require the service. Despite this, I regularly respond to leads within one or two minutes of them being posted, only to have the customer tell me they no longer need the work.

When I’ve requested my credits back in these circumstances, the requests have been refused, with the explanation that Bark cannot be responsible if a customer changes their mind. Based on my experience, around 40% of the credits I’ve purchased have been spent on customers who no longer required the service, while approximately 50% of customers never answer the phone at all.

As an emergency plumber, where customers are supposedly looking for urgent assistance, those figures simply don’t reflect what I’d expect from genuine, active leads.

My experience with Yell has been extremely disappointing and, unfortunately, what began in January 2026 remains an ongoing saga.

Immediately following a formal review of my campaign, I raised serious concerns regarding lead quality, lead classification, campaign performance and the overall value being delivered. I was informed that my Account Manager carried out an audit with his manager, both agreed there were concerns, and the matter was escalated internally. Despite this, the issues were ultimately rejected and I have yet to receive what I consider to be satisfactory evidence addressing the points raised.

A major concern was the classification of leads. I challenged whether supplier calls, missed calls, existing customers and other non-sales contacts should have been counted towards campaign performance and lead guarantee figures. Despite repeatedly requesting evidence, I do not believe these concerns have been properly addressed.

The performance of the campaign was also deeply concerning. Based on the figures provided to me by Yell, my analysis showed that the effective cost per conversion was in excess of £1,500. For any small business, that level of performance raises serious questions about campaign management, optimisation and value for money.

What makes this particularly frustrating is that since leaving Yell, my business has achieved dramatically different results. Under independent Google Ads management, I have generated more genuine enquiries and secured more new customers in approximately three months than I achieved during the eighteen months Yell managed the account. My current campaign is producing conversions at approximately £48 each and the business is now thriving.

I was also disappointed by the lack of transparency surrounding fees and advertising spend. Google publishes policies for third-party partners that emphasise transparency regarding services, fees and the management of advertising accounts. As a business owner investing significant sums each month, I believe clients should have clear visibility of where their money is being spent and exactly what value is being delivered.

Rather than reaching a satisfactory resolution, this dispute has continued since January and remains unresolved. Throughout the process I have repeatedly requested evidence to support the conclusions being presented, but I have found the responses largely consist of assertions rather than the underlying information required to independently verify the position.

Every business will have its own experience, but mine has been one of ongoing dispute, poor transparency, unresolved concerns and disappointing results relative to the investment made.

There is no lead guarantee, it should be called something else as it appeared to focus almost entirely on the quantity of enquiries rather than the quality of those enquiries.

As a business owner, I don't measure success by how many people contact me. I measure success by how many genuine opportunities are created and how many customers are won.

The impression I was left with was that once a contact had been recorded, the emphasis was on counting it towards the lead target rather than examining whether it represented a realistic sales opportunity for my business.

From my perspective, there seemed to be a significant difference between what Yell considered a lead and what I considered a genuine prospective customer.

That distinction matters because businesses do not grow from lead numbers on a report. They grow from relevant enquiries, quotations, sales and profitable work.

If a supplier call, a missed call, an existing customer, your Auntie or someone looking for a product you do not offer can all contribute towards a lead target, then business owners should look very carefully at how success is being measured before placing too much reliance on a lead guarantee.


If you are considering Yell, I would strongly recommend asking detailed questions about lead validation, campaign management, reporting transparency and exactly how your advertising budget is being allocated before signing any agreement.
Also go over their terms and conditions with a fine tooth comb before signing.

I am filing this complaint regarding Yelp’s review filtering practices and the impact they are having on my business.

Our business currently has approximately 37 five-star customer reviews that Yelp has placed in the “not recommended” section. These reviews appear to be from legitimate customers who used our services and took the time to share their experiences. However, Yelp does not include these reviews in our displayed rating, making them difficult for potential customers to find.

This creates a misleading impression of our business and does not accurately represent the feedback we have received from our customers. Yelp does not provide a clear explanation of why each review was removed from the recommended section, nor does it provide a meaningful appeal process for the business owner or reviewer.

I understand that Yelp uses automated software to identify potentially unreliable reviews. However, when dozens of legitimate five-star reviews are excluded, the system appears unfair, inaccurate, and damaging to the reputation of the business.

I am requesting that Yelp:

1. Conduct a manual review of the 37 five-star reviews currently marked as “not recommended.”
2. Provide a specific explanation for why each review was filtered.
3. Restore any reviews that were submitted by verified, legitimate customers.
4. Provide a fair and transparent appeal process for businesses affected by review filtering.
5. Correct our displayed rating to accurately reflect all legitimate customer feedback.

These reviews directly affect consumer perception, search visibility, and our ability to compete fairly. Businesses should not be financially or reputationally harmed by an automated system without transparency, accountability, or a reasonable opportunity to challenge inaccurate decisions.

I am requesting a written response explaining what Yelp will do to investigate and resolve this issue.

Dare’s Cleaning Services Limited subscribed to Checkatrade based on the representations made regarding the enquiries provided to tradespeople through the platform.

During the subscription period, Dare’s Cleaning Services Limited raised concerns regarding a number of enquiries received through the service. These concerns related to overlapping contact details and enquiries which, in the view of Dare’s Cleaning Services Limited, warranted further investigation.

In correspondence, Checkatrade explained that some situations could arise through homeowner error and indicated that duplicate submissions could not always be completely prevented. However, Checkatrade’s later court Defence stated that its investigation had identified no duplicate, non-genuine or spam leads. Dare’s Cleaning Services Limited considered this difficult to reconcile with the earlier correspondence, and it formed part of the concerns raised throughout the dispute.

Dare’s Cleaning Services Limited subsequently requested cancellation of the subscription. Dare’s Cleaning Services Limited understood from Checkatrade’s correspondence that cancellation was to be dealt with by telephone. Dare’s Cleaning Services Limited requested that communications be conducted in writing by email so that a clear and verifiable record could be maintained.

When the matter was not resolved, Dare’s Cleaning Services Limited issued a Letter Before Action and subsequently commenced County Court proceedings.

Following the commencement of proceedings, Checkatrade issued a credit memo. The matter later proceeded to a Dispute Resolution Hearing before the County Court.

At the hearing, Checkatrade confirmed to the court that the agreement/subscription had been cancelled, that no further payments were due from Dare’s Cleaning Services Limited, and that any sums allegedly due had been written off. The court order records Checkatrade’s confirmation that the agreement/subscription had been cancelled, that no further payments were due from Dare’s Cleaning Services Limited, and that any sums allegedly due had been written off. The claim was dismissed and no order as to costs was made.

The purpose of the proceedings was not primarily to recover money, but to obtain certainty that the subscription had been brought to an end and that no future debt recovery action would be pursued.

Based on this experience, tradespeople should carefully review contractual terms, maintain detailed written records, and obtain important information and confirmations in writing wherever possible. Where agreements are discussed by telephone, it may be prudent to request written confirmation of the key terms before accepting or proceeding with any agreement.

This review reflects the experience of Dare’s Cleaning Services Limited and the outcome recorded in the County Court order.

As a small business owner, I find Yelp's review system extremely frustrating and unfair. This creates a one-sided narrative that can damage the reputation of hardworking business owners who have spent years building trust in their communities.
A review platform should be focused on fairness, transparency, and factual information. Instead, it often feels as though businesses are presumed guilty while reviewers are automatically believed. Small businesses deserve a fair process to challenge false claims and provide evidence when reviews are inaccurate.
Yelp has the power to influence public perception, and with that power comes the responsibility to ensure reviews are truthful and balanced. Unfortunately, that has not been my experience.

As a small business owner, my experience with Yelp has been extremely disappointing.

Our company has been serving our community since 1948, and we've worked hard to earn our reputation through honest service and customer satisfaction. We recently discovered that more than 20 legitimate 5-star reviews from actual customers have been placed in Yelp's "Not Currently Recommended" section and do not count toward our public rating.

When I contacted Yelp Support, I was told the review recommendation system is fully automated and cannot be changed or reviewed manually. While I understand the need to prevent fake reviews, a system that hides genuine positive reviews while leaving negative reviews visible creates a misleading representation of a business's reputation.

As a result, potential customers—and even AI-powered recommendation tools—may see an inaccurate picture of our business despite hundreds of positive reviews on other platforms.

I believe Yelp should provide business owners with greater transparency about why reviews are filtered and offer a meaningful process for appealing legitimate customer reviews. Until then, I have little confidence that the rating shown on Yelp accurately reflects the quality of many businesses.

I am beyond frustrated with Yelp and the way they handle serious issues that directly damage a business’s reputation.

We recently received a negative review from someone who clearly confused our company with another business. This is not the first time — it has happened multiple times. Every time, we report it, explain the situation, and provide context. And every single time, Yelp did absolutely nothing.

This is unacceptable. Incorrect reviews are not harmless — they lower our rating, mislead potential clients, and directly impact our revenue. A platform that profits from businesses should have basic systems in place to verify or remove clearly inaccurate reviews. Yelp chooses not to.

What makes this even worse is the constant pressure to pay for advertising. Yelp has no problem calling, emailing, and pushing for higher monthly payments, yet shows zero urgency when it comes to protecting the businesses that fund their platform.

At this point, it feels like Yelp is more interested in selling visibility than maintaining fairness or accuracy. There is a clear lack of accountability, transparency, and real support.

For any business considering relying on Yelp, be aware: you may be paying to be on a platform that allows false information to harm your reputation — and does nothing to fix it.

I submitted a full listing, was told approval takes 2 days, and heard nothing for 4. I contacted customer service to chase the approval and, at the same time, clearly stated I did not want my phone number published. Nobody told me this was a problem. They said the request had been escalated to get the listing approved.

A day later I got a call that turned out to be a long, mandatory SEO sales pitch, I was asked about pricing, margins, travel radius, website traffic, and more, all framed as necessary to "list my business," while being used to push their paid services. I told the agent repeatedly, multiple times, that I did not want my number listed. He said "OK" each time. At the end of the call, he told me the listing was published. I checked the listing and found my number published, against explicit instructions I'd now given to two separate people. I went to live chat to get it removed. Instead of addressing what I'd actually said, I was met with a wall of scripted "guidelines" language, repeated regardless of what I typed. When I explicitly stated I was revoking my consent under GDPR, they didn't engage with that at all, just more guidelines, as if their internal policy overrides UK data protection law.

This isn't a case of me not understanding how the platform works. I gave clear, repeated, explicit instructions to two different people before anything was published, and was actively reassured both times. Yell published my personal data anyway, then treated a formal GDPR consent withdrawal as something to be managed with a script rather than a legal right. Followed all this up with an unsolicited email telling me what's "wrong" with my SEO.

I've now spent hours dealing with a problem they created, on top of a sales process that used data-gathering as leverage before I'd even agreed to anything.

If you're a business with any reason to keep your number off a public listing, be aware that "no" does not seem to register with their staff until it's already too late.

I submitted a job request through Checkatrade for some tarmac work on my property. I expected to receive responses from interested tradespeople that I could review and decide who I wanted to deal with.

Instead, since Saturday morning I have received approximately 20 phone calls, as well as WhatsApp messages, from different tradespeople regarding the job.

I find this incredibly intrusive. I did not expect submitting one request for quotes to result in my personal mobile number apparently being shared widely enough for me to be contacted repeatedly throughout the weekend.

To make matters worse, I tried to log into Checkatrade to close the job and stop the enquiries. Although I can see the job listed and can even see tradespeople associated with it, whenever I try to access the account-management area I am blocked by a mandatory “Complete your profile” screen asking me to provide further personal information.

So Checkatrade has enough of my information for tradespeople to phone and WhatsApp me, but I can't simply access my own job and close it without providing them with more information.

I have now had to submit a formal complaint asking Checkatrade to close the job, stop sharing my contact details and tell me how many businesses my information has been provided to.

Based on my experience, I would not use Checkatrade's quote-request service again. There needs to be much better control over who receives a customer's contact details and a simple, obvious way for customers to stop a job and further contact.
